criterion_scores.reasoning: The main ledger-scan logic and the `stop_hook_active` split are coherent, but the setup path can fail open: a bad/missing project directory exits 0 without checking anything (line 35). I checked the two execution branches, ledger parsing, and corruption handling; the core gate works, but this environment failure is a real correctness defect.

The script includes the expected scan logic, pending/corrupt handling, and both interactive and already-blocked outputs. However, it treats an empty ledger set as a clean pass (line 71), so a missing ledger file or absent writer evidence is not handled as a failure case.

The artifact follows the local shell/hook conventions reasonably well: correct shebang, JSON stdout contract, session-specific ledger plus `_pending` fallback, and no obvious naming/frontmatter issues. I did not find a convention violation worth lowering this below a normal pass-with-nits level.

This is fairly lean and avoids obvious ceremony or duplicated state. The one place it gets close to an anti-pattern is the broad fail-open behavior on environment/setup problems, but I do not see speculative surface, tombstoned decisions, or unnecessary complexity.

The emitted messages are specific and the failure text is actionable, but the durability path swallows write errors (line 126), so the claimed persistent audit trail can disappear without any operator-visible signal. I checked the error surfaces and the logged record path; the messaging is good, but not fully honest about write failures.

defects.description: If the hook cannot change into the project directory, it silently exits 0 and never checks any ledger. For a gate whose job is to prevent silently skipped Deep Reads from closing green, this is a fail-open path.

defects.quote: [ "${#LEDGERS[@]}" -eq 0 ] && exit 0   # no ledger → run touched no events → nothing to gate
defects.description: An empty ledger set is treated as a clean pass, so a missing or never-written ledger is indistinguishable from a genuinely empty session. That leaves the exact silent-skip failure mode this hook is meant to catch unhandled.
The append that is supposed to make the failure durable suppresses write errors, so the audit record can fail silently and operators get no indication that the after-the-fact log was not persisted.
